Final Project - PSTAT 131

Ellie Huang

12-08-2024

Introduction

In the realm of online multiplayer games, League of Legends stands out as one of the most popular and competitive titles, engaging millions of players worldwide in fast-paced, team-based battles. Each match in League of Legends pits two teams of five players against each other, with the primary objective being to destroy the enemy’s Nexus, a critical structure located at the heart of their base. Players control champions, unique characters with specific abilities, roles, and attributes that contribute to the team’s strategy and performance. Throughout the game, players accumulate experience points (XP), gold, and items, all of which enhance their champion’s abilities and influence their impact on the match.

A central performance metric in League of Legends is the Kill/Death/Assist (KDA) ratio, which quantifies a player’s effectiveness by balancing their offensive contributions (kills and assists) against their defensive responsibility (avoiding deaths). High KDA ratios are generally associated with skilled gameplay and strategic awareness, making KDA a valuable indicator for analyzing performance. This project is focused on the statistics taken from players ranked Master and above, in the North America (NA) region. The primary goal of this project is to build a model that can predict a player’s KDA based on various in-game factors, such as gold earned, role, and match duration. By examining these variables, my aim is to uncover patterns that influence KDA and contribute to a deeper understanding of gameplay dynamics.

Source of Data

The data for this project was sourced from the Riot Games Developer API (Riot Games, Inc., 2024), which provides comprehensive in-game statistics for League of Legends. 1497 observations of key metrics such as match history, champion stats, and player rankings were collected to support KDA prediction analysis. Data access required an API key, with relevant match data filtered for this project’s focus.

For API details, visit the Riot Games Developer Portal: https://developer.riotgames.com/.

Citation: Riot Games, Inc. (2024). Riot Games Developer Portal. https://developer.riotgames.com/.

A codebook of variables and their descriptions are attached as a separate .doc file.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

Missing data

There seems to be a lot of missing data for neutral_minions_killed, since this statistic is specific to a certain player role, this variable should be removed. There is also missing data for vision score, so I will remove the observations that are NA. For wards_placed and wards_killed, they will be removed later in the process (they are highly correlated with vision_score and thus should be removed). There also looks to be a lot of missing data for total_heals_on_teammates and total_damage_shielded_on_teammates, so I will remove those variables as well. This also makes sense because heals and damage shielded on teammates doesn’t seem to be exactly relevant to the a player’s KDA/individual performance.

player_stats <- read.csv("player_stats.csv")
player_stats <- player_stats %>% 
  select(-X)
naniar::vis_miss(player_stats)

player_stats <- player_stats %>% 
  select(-neutral_minions_killed, -total_heals_on_teammates, -total_damage_shielded_on_teammates) %>% 
  drop_na() # remove rows with NA obs

naniar::vis_miss(player_stats)

Visualize distribution for KDA

# Histogram for KDA components
ggplot(player_stats, aes(x = kills)) + 
  geom_histogram(color = "white", fill = "steelblue") + 
  ggtitle("Distribution of Kills")

ggplot(player_stats, aes(x = deaths)) + 
  geom_histogram(color = "white", fill = "steelblue") + 
  ggtitle("Distribution of Deaths")

ggplot(player_stats, aes(x = assists)) + 
  geom_histogram(color = "white", fill = "steelblue") + 
  ggtitle("Distribution of Assists")

# Now, calculate the KDA variable = (kills + assists)/deaths to the dataset and remove kills, deaths, and assists because they would be redundant, since each is directly used to calculate the KDA.

player_stats <- player_stats %>%
  mutate(kda = if_else(deaths > 0, (kills + assists) / deaths, kills + assists))

summary(player_stats$kda)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   0.000   1.667   2.875   4.209   5.000  33.000
ggplot(player_stats, aes(x = kda)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Player KDA", x = "KDA", y = "Count")

KDA looks to be heavily right skewed, with the median being 2.875, and the most players having a KDA between 1 and 5. Similarly, the separate stats of kills, deaths, and assists were also right skewed.

KDA relationships

fig_1 <- player_stats %>%
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(kda, kills, deaths, assists), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Value, y = kda)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
  labs(title = "Relationships with KDA", x = "Value", y = "KDA")

ggsave("relationships_with_kda.png", fig_1, width = 20, height = 15)

The predictors’ relationships with KDA looks to be quite nonlinear, suggesting that we should use regression models that are better for working with nonlinear data, such as random forest, rather than linear regression models.

Categorical Variables

player_stats <- player_stats %>% 
  mutate(lane = as.factor(lane))

player_stats %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = lane)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Lane", x = "Lane", y = "Count") + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

We convert the character variable to factor. Looking at the distribution of the categorical variable, the most selected role was Bottom, with over 300 players, and the least selected role was Fill, with less than 100 players.

Correlation

numeric_columns <- player_stats %>% 
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>% 
  select(-c(kills, assists, deaths))

cor_matrix <- cor(numeric_columns)
corrplot(cor_matrix, "circle", type = "lower", tl.cex = 0.6, tl.srt = 45)

# Identify pairs of columns with correlation > 0.9
high_corr_pairs <- which(abs(cor_matrix) > 0.9, arr.ind = TRUE)

# Exclude self-correlations
high_corr_pairs <- high_corr_pairs[high_corr_pairs[, 1] != high_corr_pairs[, 2], ]

# Review and decide which columns to drop
print(high_corr_pairs)
##              row col
## wards_placed   9   8
## vision_score   8   9
player_stats <- player_stats %>% 
  select(-wards_placed, -wards_killed, -total_damage_dealt_to_champions)

The correlation matrix revealed that the most predictive variables for KDA are longest_time_spent_living, damage_dealt_to_objectives, and total_damage_dealt_to_champions, all of which showed strong positive correlations. These findings suggest that KDA is primarily influenced by survivability, objective contribution, and impactful gameplay in team fights, which are key to player performance. In contrast, variables such as total_minions_killed and lane demonstrated weak correlations, indicating that early-game farming and lane position have limited direct impact on KDA compared to mid-to-late-game actions.

Total_damage_dealt_to_champions is highly correlated with damage_dealt_to_objectives and gold_earned is correlated with total_damage_taken. I removed wards_placed, as well as wards_killed, because those directly contribute to vision score, indicating high multicollinearity/redundancy in those variables.

Outliers

fig_2 <- player_stats %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = where(is.numeric), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Variable, y = Value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "blue", alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free", ncol = 2) + 
  labs(title = "Outlier Detection by Variable", x = "Variable", y = "Value") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), 
    strip.text = element_text(size = 10), 
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

ggsave("outliers.png", fig_2, width = 20, height = 15)

The variables with clear outliers are damage_dealt_to_objectives, damage_self_mitigated, and longest_time_spent_living.

cap_outliers <- function(variable) {
  Q1 <- quantile(variable, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
  Q3 <- quantile(variable, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  IQR <- Q3 - Q1
  lower_bound <- Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
  upper_bound <- Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
  variable <- ifelse(variable < lower_bound, lower_bound,
                     ifelse(variable > upper_bound, upper_bound, variable))
  return(variable)
}

predictors <- c("damage_dealt_to_objectives", "longest_time_spent_living",
                "gold_earned", "total_damage_taken",
                "total_heal", "vision_score")

# Apply IQR method to cap outliers
player_stats <- player_stats %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(predictors), cap_outliers))

Since I intend to evaluate my models on metrics like RMSE and MSE, which are sensitive to large errors and are often caused by outliers, capping can lead to fairer evaluations of model performance.

Testing/Training Split

player_split <- initial_split(player_stats, prop = 0.8, strata = kda)

player_train <- training(player_split)
player_test <- testing(player_split)

Recipe

player_recipe <- recipe(kda ~ damage_dealt_to_objectives + 
                                  damage_self_mitigated + 
                                  total_damage_taken + 
                                  gold_earned + 
                                  total_minions_killed + 
                                  lane + 
                                  time_played + 
                                  vision_score + 
                                  longest_time_spent_living + 
                                  total_heal + 
                                  time_c_cing_others, 
                        data = player_train) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

K-fold Cross Validation

folds <- vfold_cv(player_train, v = 5, strata = kda)

Define Models - Elastic Net, Random Forest, Gradient Boosted Trees, Support Vector Machines

elastic_net_model <- linear_reg(
  penalty = tune(),  # Regularization strength
  mixture = tune()   # Balance between Ridge (0) and Lasso (1)
) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet")

rf_model <- rand_forest(
  mtry = tune(),         # Number of variables to try at each split
  trees = tune(),          # Number of trees
  min_n = tune()         # Minimum data points in a node
) %>%
  set_engine("ranger") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

gbt_model <- boost_tree(
  trees = tune(),         # Number of trees
  learn_rate = tune(),  # Learning rate
  tree_depth = tune()   # Maximum tree depth
) %>%
  set_engine("xgboost") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

svm_model <- svm_rbf(
  cost = tune(),      # Regularization parameter
  rbf_sigma = tune()  # Kernel parameter
) %>%
  set_engine("kernlab") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

metric = metric_set(rmse)

Applying Models to Player Data

# Workflow
elastic_net_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(player_recipe) %>%
  add_model(elastic_net_model)

# Define Grid for Hyperparameter Tuning
elastic_net_grid <- grid_regular(
  penalty(range = c(0.0001, 1)),
  mixture(range = c(0, 1)),
  levels = 5
)

elastic_net_results <- tune_grid(
  elastic_net_workflow,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = elastic_net_grid,
  metrics = metric # Metrics for evaluation
)

autoplot(elastic_net_results)

elastic_net_metrics <- elastic_net_results %>%
  collect_metrics() %>%
  filter(.metric == "rmse") %>% 
  mutate(mse = mean^2)

library(vip)

best_vars <- best_rf %>% 
  select(mtry, trees, min_n)

best_rf_vars <- rand_forest(
  mtry = best_vars$mtry,
  trees = best_vars$trees,
  min_n = best_vars$min_n
) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

best_rf_fit <- best_rf_vars %>%
  fit(kda ~ damage_dealt_to_objectives + 
                                  damage_self_mitigated + 
                                  total_damage_taken + 
                                  gold_earned + 
                                  total_minions_killed + 
                                  lane + 
                                  time_played + 
                                  vision_score + 
                                  longest_time_spent_living + 
                                  total_heal + 
                                  time_c_cing_others, data = player_train)

vip(best_rf_fit$fit, num_features = 12, geom = "col", aesthetics = list(color = "black", fill = "lavender")) +
  labs(title = "Variable Importance Plot for Best-Performing Random Forest Model")

The variables longest_time_spent_living, total_damage_taken, and damage_dealt_to_objectives were found to be the most significant predictors of KDA, likely reflecting a player’s skill and contribution to team objectives. On the other hand, lane and vision_score contributed little to the model’s predictive accuracy, suggesting their limited relevance to performance in terms of KDA. This might diminish the importance of the initial lane assignment for predicting overall performance. This is consistent with the results of the correlation matrix of predictors, which can be found in the EDA section.

# Workflow for SVM
svm_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(player_recipe) %>%
  add_model(svm_model)

# Hyperparameter tuning
svm_grid <- grid_regular(
  cost(range = c(0.1, 100)),
  rbf_sigma(range = c(0.01, 1)),
  levels = 5
)

svm_results <- tune_grid(
  svm_workflow,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = svm_grid,
  metrics = metric
)

autoplot(svm_results)

svm_metrics <- svm_results %>%
  collect_metrics() %>%
  filter(.metric == "rmse") %>%
  mutate(mse = mean^2)

print(svm_metrics)

Fitting the best model to the testing set

Althought the updated random forest model had the lowest MSE, it was by a margin, and considering that the other models performed worse with the lane variable dropped, we will proceed with the original random forest model to fit to the testing set.

best_model_params <- rf_results %>%
  select_best()

best_model_workflow <- rf_workflow %>%
  finalize_workflow(best_model_params)

final_fit <- best_model_workflow %>%
  fit(data = player_test)

rf_predictions <- predict(final_fit, new_data = player_test) %>%
  bind_cols(player_test)

Testing error of the best model

rf_testing_error <- rf_predictions %>%
  metrics(truth = kda, estimate = .pred)

rf_testing_error
## # A tibble: 3 × 3
##   .metric .estimator .estimate
##   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
## 1 rmse    standard       1.48 
## 2 rsq     standard       0.968
## 3 mae     standard       0.869

The RMSE of the random forest model fitted to the testing set is around 1.55. An RMSE of 1.55 indicates that, on average, the model predicts a player’s KDA with an error of about 1.55 units.

Conclusion

This analysis highlights the random forest model as the most effective approach for predicting KDA, achieving an RMSE of 1.55 on the testing set. The model’s superior performance underscores its ability to capture complex, non-linear relationships and interactions between predictors. Key features such as longest_time_spent_living, damage_dealt_to_objectives, and total_damage_dealt_to_champions were strongly correlated with KDA, emphasizing the importance of survivability, objective contributions, and impactful gameplay during team fights. In contrast, variables like lane and vision_score demonstrated limited predictive power, with their removal marginally improving the random forest model while negatively affecting others.

Despite these findings, efforts to improve model performance through variable selection and tuning resulted in only marginal gains. This suggests that further experimentation with feature engineering, such as creating new variables to capture nuanced gameplay dynamics or interactions, may be necessary to unlock more significant improvements.Additionally, the quality of the dataset may have constrained the models’ predictive power. Moving forward, implementing more robust data collection methods—such as integrating larger, more diverse samples could provide richer information for analysis. Enhanced data preprocessing techniques, such as addressing potential biases or capturing additional game-specific metrics, might also yield better results. By refining both feature engineering and data collection processes, future models could not only achieve higher accuracy but also provide deeper insights into the factors driving player performance.
